about.heading: About hepatitis B, hepatitis C and testing

questions.question: What are hepatitis B and hepatitis C?
questions.answer:
Hepatitis B and hepatitis C are viruses that infect the liver. Both can spread through blood, and hepatitis B can also be passed on through sex, which is why it’s often included in STI testing. Many people with either virus have no symptoms, so they don’t know they have it.

A hepatitis B and C home test kit lets you check for both at once. You use a small finger-prick of blood, and the test shows a separate result for each in around 15 minutes, with nothing to post to a lab.

questions.question: How are hepatitis B and C passed on?
questions.answer: Both viruses spread through infected blood. Hepatitis B is also found in semen and vaginal fluid, so it can be passed on through sex without a condom. Hepatitis C is rarely passed on through sex, but the risk is higher if blood is present, such as during anal sex. Neither virus spreads through kissing, hugging, coughing or sharing cups.

questions.question: What are the symptoms of hepatitis?
questions.answer:
Many people have no symptoms, sometimes for years. When symptoms do appear, they can include:

  • Tiredness and flu-like symptoms
  • Pain in the upper tummy
  • Feeling or being sick, and loss of appetite
  • Yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes (jaundice), which can be harder to see on brown or black skin
  • Dark pee and pale poo

Because symptoms are often missing, a blood test is the only way to know.

questions.question: Can hepatitis B and C be treated?
questions.answer: Yes. Most adults clear hepatitis B on their own, and long-term hepatitis B can be managed with medicine and regular check-ups. Hepatitis C can be cured in most people with antiviral tablets taken for 8 to 12 weeks. Left untreated for many years, both can cause liver scarring (cirrhosis) and raise the risk of liver cancer, so finding them early matters.

questions.question: Who should take a hepatitis B and C test?
questions.answer:
You don’t need symptoms to test. It may be worth testing if:

  • You’ve had sex without a condom
  • You have a new sexual partner, or more than one partner
  • A sexual partner has told you they have hepatitis B, hepatitis C or another STI
  • You’ve ever shared needles or other injecting equipment
  • You’d prefer to test privately at home

Have symptoms, or a partner has tested positive? Contact your GP or a sexual health clinic now.

accordions.content:
Hepatitis B and hepatitis C are viruses that affect the liver. Hepatitis B can be passed on through sex without a condom, and both can be passed on through blood, for example by sharing needles. They can cause symptoms such as tiredness, a high temperature or yellowing of the skin and eyes, but many people have no noticeable symptoms at all.

Many adults recover from a new hepatitis B infection on their own within a few months. Some develop a long-term infection that needs monitoring or treatment. Hepatitis C can usually be cured with antiviral tablets.

how.heading: How does the hepatitis B and C home test work?
how.intro:
The test checks a small finger-prick blood sample for two things, and shows each in its own window:

  • Hepatitis B (HBsAg window): looks for hepatitis B surface antigen, a part of the virus. A positive may mean a current infection.
  • Hepatitis C (HCV window): looks for hepatitis C antibodies, which your body makes after contact with the virus. These can stay in your blood even after the infection has cleared or been treated.

Your results appear in around 15 minutes, with no sample to send to a lab.
how.stepsHeading: How to use the hepatitis B and C test kit in 3 steps

steps.title: Prick your finger
steps.text: Wash your hands and clean your fingertip with an alcohol pad. Let it dry, then use the lancet to prick your finger and form a drop of blood.

image.alt: Step 2 add blood and diluent to each well

steps.title: Add blood and diluent
steps.text: Use the pipette to collect your blood. Add 3 drops of blood to each sample well on the test pad, then 2 drops of diluent (test liquid) to each well.

image.alt: Step 3 read your hepatitis B and C results

steps.title: Read your results
steps.text: Read both windows between 15 and 20 minutes. Don’t read them after 30 minutes, as the results may no longer be reliable.

results.heading: How to read your hepatitis B and C test result

groups.intro: Read both windows between 15 and 20 minutes. Don’t read them after 30 minutes. The HBsAg window shows hepatitis B and the HCV window shows hepatitis C. In each window, C is the control line and T is the test line.

image.alt: Negative result, C line only in both windows

items.title: Negative for both
items.text: One line at C only in both windows. No hepatitis B surface antigen or hepatitis C antibodies were detected.

image.alt: Hepatitis B positive, C and T lines in the HBsAg window

items.title: Hepatitis B positive
items.text: Lines at C and T in the HBsAg window, even if the T line is faint. Hepatitis B surface antigen was detected, which may indicate a current infection.

image.alt: Hepatitis C positive, C and T lines in the HCV window

items.title: Hepatitis C positive
items.text: Lines at C and T in the HCV window, even if the T line is faint. Hepatitis C antibodies were detected, which may indicate a current or past infection.

items.title: Invalid
items.text: No line at C in one or both windows, even if a T line appears. The test has not worked. Contact us and we’ll help.

notes.text:
If both windows show lines at C and T, both results are positive.

A positive result always needs a follow-up test with your GP or a sexual health clinic to confirm it.

faq.heading: Hepatitis B and C home test FAQs

questions.question: How soon after exposure can I test for hepatitis B and C?
questions.answer: You can test now, but an early negative may need repeating at 12 weeks after exposure for hepatitis B and six months for hepatitis C. If you have symptoms, know you’ve been exposed or want advice about testing sooner, contact your GP or a sexual health clinic.

questions.question: How reliable is the hepatitis B and C home test?
questions.answer: When used correctly, this is a reliable screening test. Testing too soon after exposure can affect your result. A positive result needs a follow-up test with your GP or a sexual health clinic to confirm it.

questions.question: How do I use the hepatitis B and C home test kit?
questions.answer: Clean and prick your fingertip, then add 3 drops of blood and 2 drops of diluent to each sample well. Read both windows between 15 and 20 minutes. Everything you need is in the box.

questions.question: Does this test show hepatitis B and C separately?
questions.answer: Yes. The test has two windows: HBsAg for hepatitis B and HCV for hepatitis C. Each gives its own result, so you’ll know which one, if either, was detected.

questions.question: What does a negative result mean?
questions.answer: A negative result means hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibodies were not detected. If your possible exposure was recent, an early negative may need repeating at 12 weeks for hepatitis B and six months for hepatitis C, counted from your last possible exposure. If you have symptoms or concerns, speak to your GP or a sexual health clinic.

questions.question: What if my result is positive?
questions.answer: You’ll need a follow-up test with your GP or a sexual health clinic to understand what it means. A hepatitis B positive may mean a current infection. A hepatitis C positive may mean a current or past infection. NHS sexual health services are free and confidential.

questions.question: Can I use this test if I’ve had the hepatitis B vaccine?
questions.answer: Yes. The vaccine shouldn’t cause a positive result, because the test looks for a part of the virus, not the antibodies the vaccine makes. This also means the test can’t show whether you’re immune.

questions.question: Can I use this test if I’ve had hepatitis C before?
questions.answer: You can, but the HCV result may still be positive, because hepatitis C antibodies can stay in your blood after the infection has gone. Your GP or a clinic can arrange an HCV RNA test to check for active virus.

questions.question: Can I take this test while pregnant?
questions.answer: Speak to your midwife, GP or a sexual health clinic. Hepatitis B testing is routinely offered during pregnancy through the NHS.

questions.question: What are the first signs of hepatitis B?
questions.answer: Many people have no signs at all. When symptoms do appear, they can include tiredness, fever, pain in the upper tummy, feeling sick, dark pee and yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice).

questions.question: What are the first signs of hepatitis C?
questions.answer: Most people have no signs for years. Some get flu-like symptoms, tiredness, tummy pain, loss of appetite or feel sick. Because signs are often missing, a blood test is the only way to know.

questions.question: What’s the difference between hepatitis B and C?
questions.answer: Both infect the liver, but hepatitis B spreads more easily through sex, while hepatitis C spreads mainly through blood. There’s a vaccine for hepatitis B but not for hepatitis C. Hepatitis C can be cured with tablets in most people, and most adults clear hepatitis B on their own.

questions.question: How is hepatitis C spread?
questions.answer: Hepatitis C spreads mainly through blood-to-blood contact. The most common way is sharing needles or other injecting equipment. It can also spread by sharing razors or toothbrushes, and from mother to baby.

questions.question: Can you get hepatitis C from sex?
questions.answer: It’s possible but rare. The risk is higher if blood is present, such as during anal sex. Using condoms with new partners and for anal sex lowers the risk.

questions.question: Is hepatitis C curable?
questions.answer: Yes. Antiviral tablets taken every day for 8 to 12 weeks can cure hepatitis C in most people. Treatment is available on the NHS.

questions.question: Can you get hepatitis C more than once?
questions.answer: Yes. Being cured doesn’t stop you catching hepatitis C again, so it’s still important to avoid sharing needles, razors or toothbrushes.

questions.question: Can hepatitis B be cured?
questions.answer: Most adults clear hepatitis B on their own within a few months and are then usually immune. If the infection lasts longer than 6 months, it’s called chronic hepatitis B. This can’t usually be cured, but medicine can control the virus and protect the liver.

questions.question: Is there a vaccine for hepatitis?
questions.answer: There’s a vaccine for hepatitis B, which is part of the UK childhood vaccination programme and is offered to people at higher risk. There’s no vaccine for hepatitis C.

questions.question: What happens if hepatitis is left untreated?
questions.answer: Over many years, long-term hepatitis B or C can scar the liver (cirrhosis) and raise the risk of liver failure and liver cancer. Testing and treating early lowers these risks.

questions.question: Can you catch hepatitis from kissing?
questions.answer: No. Hepatitis B and C don’t spread through kissing, hugging, holding hands, coughing or sharing cups and cutlery.

questions.question: Will anyone know what I ordered?
questions.answer: No. Your order arrives in plain, discreet packaging with nothing on the outside to reveal what’s inside. Click & Collect is also available at checkout. Your bank statement won’t show “Test Discreet” or the name of the test.

questions.question: Can I get a free hepatitis test on the NHS?
questions.answer: Yes. Your GP or an NHS sexual health clinic can test you for free and confidentially. Many people choose a rapid home test for a result in 15 minutes, with no appointment and no sample to post.

questions.question: Does this test check for other STIs?
questions.answer: No, this kit only tests for hepatitis B and C. If you may have been exposed to one infection, you may have been exposed to others, such as HIV, which can also spread through shared needles, or syphilis, chlamydia and gonorrhoea and genital herpes.
